extra.text: An engineer expects a small step in the input to give a small step in the score. Bayesian optimisation builds that expectation into its model: Gaussian processes rely on the smoothness defined by a kernel, Oh et al. 2019, Section 1, https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.00448. On Pest Control, a benchmark from that paper, one step moves the score by 0.14 of that benchmark's spread when the spread is pooled, or 0.37 and 0.32 when each kind of starting point uses its own spread, source: v2/FACTS.md, Reading two, and rerun-readings.json, pest_control. No paper found says benchmarks are smooth because methods need smoothness. That link is an inference. Decided 2026-11-13: the two kinds of starting point are not pooled, so the step is 0.37 and 0.32 and the pooled 0.14 is not used.

owner_answers.label: The reader's default, defined
owner_answers.text: The reader is an engineer or student who has trained a model or tuned one with an optimiser, but has never built a Pokemon team. Their default is that when one input changes by one small step, the score moves only a little, so points that sit close together score close together. That habit comes from the methods they use: gradient descent walks downhill one small step at a time, and Bayesian optimisation models a black-box score with a Gaussian process, which in the words of Oh et al. 2019 relies "on the smoothness defined by a kernel to model uncertainty". Pest Control, the benchmark from that same paper, behaves this way, since one changed station moves its score by a small share of the spread between its points.
